findings.problem: file I/O (fs::read_to_string), logging (println!), allocation (Vec::collect), and domain construction (Record) are fused in a single function; the functional core leaks shell concerns into pure logic
findings.failure_mode: the parser cannot be tested in isolation, cannot be composed into larger pipelines, and couples async/I/O concerns to pure data transformation
findings.fix: split into a pure parse_line(line: &str) -> Result<Record, ParseError> and a shell function load_packets(path: &str) -> Result<Vec<Record>, LoadError> that handles fs::read_to_string and iteration

findings.problem: fs::read_to_string(path).unwrap() - unwrap on fallible file I/O
findings.failure_mode: missing file, permission errors, or unreadable paths cause a synchronous panic instead of returning a typed error the caller can handle
findings.fix: return Result<Vec<Record>, LoadError> and propagate with ? or explicit map_err to a typed I/O error variant

findings.problem: parts[1].parse::<u32>().unwrap() - unwrap on fallible numeric parse
findings.failure_mode: malformed numeric fields in packet data cause a synchronous panic, aborting the entire packet load instead of reporting which record was invalid
findings.fix: parse with .map_err(|e| ParseError::InvalidValue(parts[0].clone())) and return Result<Record, ParseError>

findings.problem: parts[0] - unchecked indexing into split result with no bounds check
findings.failure_mode: empty lines or lines with fewer than 2 comma-separated fields panic at runtime with index-out-of-bounds
findings.fix: use split_once(',') to destructure into exactly two fields and handle the None case with a typed Invalid error

findings.problem: parts[1] - unchecked indexing into split result with no bounds check
findings.failure_mode: lines with only one field (no comma) panic at runtime with index-out-of-bounds when accessing parts[1]
findings.fix: use split_once(',') so the two fields are structurally guaranteed or the None branch handles the error

findings.problem: parts[1].parse::<u32>().unwrap() as u16 - lossy as conversion from u32 to u16 after parsing
findings.failure_mode: values in range 256..=4294967295 silently truncate to u16 range, corrupting data without any error or validation at the parse boundary
findings.fix: parse directly as u16 with .parse::<u16>() or use u16::try_from(u32_val).map_err(|_| ParseError::ValueOutOfBounds) for a checked widening-to-narrowing conversion

findings.problem: println!("loaded {}", parts[0]) - logging inside pure parsing logic
findings.failure_mode: side-effecting I/O in the core function makes it impure, breaks deterministic testing, and couples domain logic to console output which may be undesirable in libraries or embedded contexts
findings.fix: remove println! entirely from the parser; if diagnostics are needed, have the shell caller log after successful parse, using the Result type to carry record names

findings.problem: load_packets returns unbounded Vec<Record> with no max_items cap, no try_reserve, and no external-input size validation before allocation
findings.failure_mode: an attacker or misconfigured file with millions of lines triggers unbounded heap allocation, potentially causing OOM kill of the process or denial of service
findings.fix: add max_items: usize parameter, validate file line count or track count during iteration with count.checked_add(1), enforce count <= max_items, allocate with Vec::new() then out.try_reserve(max_items).map_err(|_| ParseError::Allocation) before the push loop

missing_evidence: no benchmark exists for packet loading performance
no profiler evidence for allocation hot path
no allocation analysis (e.g., valgrind/dhat/Rust allocation tracing) for Vec growth under typical input sizes
no second-ring evidence for any performance or zero-cost claim (none stated, but absence of benchmarks makes any future perf claim unverifiable)
no command-line interface entry point; function is a library API with no CLI harness for end-to-end evidence
residual_risk: static review only; no commands run. All eight findings are BLOCKER-severity violations of absolute Holzman Rust laws (no unwrap, no unchecked indexing, no lossy conversions, no hidden I/O, no unbounded allocation, functional-core/shell separation). The code must be repaired before any delivery gate. A typed error enum, split_once-based parsing, checked narrowing, removal of println!, I/O separation into a shell function, and bounded allocation with try_reserve are required.
